explanations.answer: Jesus Christ and God the Father
explanations.explanation: That's the whole badge, baker. Paul, the apostle writing this letter, says he was "sent not from men nor by man, but by Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised Him from the dead." He doesn't open with a résumé or a list of references. He opens with the One who sent him.
I get the thinking, friend. Apostles sound official. But Paul says he was "sent not from men nor by man," and the apostles in Jerusalem are men. The name he gives is Jesus Christ and God the Father.

Nope, and Paul shuts that door fast. The high priest, Israel's chief priest, is a man, and Paul says he was "sent not from men nor by man." He names Jesus Christ and God the Father instead. Nobody in this opening line has a desk in Jerusalem.
Right on the money. Paul says he was sent by "Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised Him from the dead." Look who he points to first thing in the letter. He's sent by the One who raised Jesus.

Let's check the text, friend. Paul says it right there in verse 1: sent by "Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised Him from the dead." So God the Father is the One who raised Jesus. That line is in the very first sentence, so it's easy to blink and miss.
Yes, sins. Paul says Jesus "gave Himself for our sins to rescue us from the present evil age." That's a rescue, baker. Jesus gave Himself for us.
Close to the right neighborhood, but the word isn't leaders. Paul says Jesus "gave Himself for our sins." Nobody gets voted out in this verse. It's a rescue from the present evil age.

I see where that came from, friend. Land comes up all over the Bible, but not in this verse. Paul says Jesus "gave Himself for our sins to rescue us from the present evil age." It's sins, and it's a rescue.
Let's read that verse again together, baker. Paul says Jesus gave Himself for our sins "according to the will of our God and Father." So it's not against the Father's will. It's according to it.

That's it, baker. Paul says Jesus gave Himself for our sins "according to the will of our God and Father." Not against it, according to it. And then Paul ends the thought with praise: "to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen."

You read Paul's tone just right. He writes, "I am amazed how quickly you are deserting the One who called you by the grace of Christ." The word is quickly. I'd say that's Paul shaking his head at the speed of it.

explanations.answer: How slowly their churches are growing
explanations.explanation: Nothing about growth speed in this letter opening, friend. Paul's amazed at how quickly the Galatians are "deserting the One who called you by the grace of Christ." The speed he's talking about is how fast they're leaving, not how slow they're growing.

explanations.answer: How rarely they've written to him
explanations.explanation: Paul's not checking his mailbox in this verse, baker. He says, "I am amazed how quickly you are deserting the One who called you by the grace of Christ." It's about the Galatians turning away, and it's about how fast they're doing it. Nobody's counting letters.
That's the one. Paul says they "are turning to a different gospel." Notice who they're deserting, too: the One who called them by the grace of Christ.
Good guess, but Paul doesn't say prophecy anywhere here. He says they are "turning to a different gospel." That's the thing that has him amazed.
Sounds mysterious, friend, but that's not in the text. Paul says they are "turning to a different gospel." Nothing secret here, just a different gospel, and Paul is not happy about it.
Hold on, baker, Paul says the opposite. The different gospel is "not even a gospel." It isn't another version of the good news. Paul doesn't give it that much credit.

Yes. Paul says this different gospel is "not even a gospel." He doesn't call it a second flavor or a remix. Then he says that some people are troubling them and trying to distort the gospel of Christ.

Distort is the word. Paul says some people are "troubling you and trying to distort the gospel of Christ." Think of a stamp pressed crooked so the cookie comes out wrong. I know a thing or two about blurry stamps, believe me.
Wouldn't that be nice, baker. But Paul says these people are "troubling you and trying to distort the gospel of Christ." Troubling and distorting are the opposite of protecting.
Honor is a good word, friend, but it's not Paul's word here. He says they are "troubling you and trying to distort the gospel of Christ." People who honor something don't go around twisting it.

That's the surprise, baker. Paul says, "But even if we or an angel from heaven should preach a gospel contrary to the one we preached to you, let him be under a curse!" He includes himself and an angel from heaven. The message itself is what matters, no matter who brings it.

Not a prophet, friend, and Jerusalem isn't mentioned in this warning at all. Paul says, "even if we or an angel from heaven should preach a gospel contrary to the one we preached to you, let him be under a curse!" The one he adds is an angel from heaven.

No kings in this one, baker. Paul says, "even if we or an angel from heaven should preach a gospel contrary to the one we preached to you, let him be under a curse!" He names himself and an angel from heaven, and that's the whole list.

That's it. Paul writes, "If I were still trying to please men, I would not be a servant of Christ." Right before that he asks, "Am I now seeking the approval of men, or of God?" He knows whose servant he is.
Moses, Israel's leader, is a big name, friend, but he's not in this verse. Paul says, "If I were still trying to please men, I would not be a servant of Christ." Christ is the One he serves.
Caesar, Rome's emperor, doesn't show up anywhere in this passage, baker. Paul says, "If I were still trying to please men, I would not be a servant of Christ." His answer is Christ.
